pages.text: Glass breaks from its surface: a scratch is a crack waiting. Temper it and the surface is squeezed shut. Glass is heated to about 620 °C, just short of softening, and both faces are blown hard with air.
pages.title: Toughened glass

pages.text: The skin sets first; the core, cooling after it, shrinks and pulls the skin into compression, so a crack must first overcome that squeeze. Tempered glass bends four or five times as far before it breaks, and when it does go it crumbles to blunt cubes, not blades.

Glass or a glass pane in a furnace, or blasted by a fan over lava, comes out hot glass; a spout of 250 mB of The Factory's air quenches a block to tempered glass, and 100 mB a pane. Tempered glass cannot be cut afterwards: the first cut lets the stress go and the whole sheet bursts.
pages.title: Tempering

pages.text: So panes are cut first and then tempered, as they are in every glass works. Tempered glass shrugs off a blast that would take out stone, at a distance.

Seen through a polarising filter, sunglasses on a car's back window, tempered glass shows a grid of dark spots: the marks of the air jets that quenched it. Sources: Gardon, "Thermal Tempering of Glass", in Glass: Science and Technology 5 (1980); EN 12150-1.
pages.title: Quench marks
